2.text: Cases like this happen in modern life, and I will describe some later on.

3.text: Of course, in order to inflict a chastisement of such a kind on the offender,

4.text: one must be able to overcome him in a struggle. Whenever I mentioned

5.text: this to my Chukchee friends, they would instantly answer, “A wronged man

6.text: will be victorious.” This is the leading idea of all ordeals and of single com-

7.text: bats for the sake of law. In actual life some encounters of this kind have

8.text: issues of exactly opposite character. Thus one of the three brother-avengers

9.text: of whom I spoke before, Vaatuˊwg̣ê by name, while still quite young, had a

10.text: drunken brawl with another young Chukchee, whose name was Peñeˊwg̣i.

11.text: They had a wrestling-match; and Vaatuˊwg̣ê, who was by far the stronger,

12.text: threw his adversary down, and, seizing one of his legs, pulled it violently and

13.text: drew it out of the socket. In consequence of this act, Peñeˊwg̣i remained lame

14.text: until his death. Now, Peñeˊwg̣i was of a meek disposition; and his cousin

15.text: Peñelquˊt, though cross-tempered enough, was but an indifferent fighter. The

16.text: offender, on the contrary, was one of the three brothers who had prepared

17.text: for murder from their youth up, and all three were strong and nimble men;

18.text: so that the wrong of Peñeˊwg̣i was left without retaliation.

19.text: Another case within my knowledge happened in the country of the Upper

20.text: Anui River, while I was travelling there. One man, Uˊmkuum by name, took

21.text: a liking to a young woman, the wife of another Chukchee, Oˊoqai, who lived

22.text: in a neighboring camp. The young woman refused his courtship; but at last

23.text: he came to her house in the absence of her husband, caught her in the en-

24.text: trance of the outer tent, and violated her. This was done in broad daylight

25.text: and in the middle of the camp. He promised to give her for this a new

26.text: seal-skin, but failed to fulfil his promise. Then she complained to her husband,

27.text: who challenged the offender to a wrestling-match; but both men proved to

28.text: be of equal physical strength. The wronged man belonged to a strong family;

29.text: and the number of his brothers, all full-grown and active, was seven. Shortly

30.text: after that, four of the best reindeer of Uˊmkuum were lost. The people in

31.text: the camps around laughed, and said that they were sold off for a single

33.text: In a camp of the Anui country, two young men had a quarrel while

34.text: playing cards. A wrestling-match followed, and the one who considered him-

35.text: self wronged threw his adversary to the ground. The vanquished one sprang

36.text: up and seized a large piece of wood that had been prepared to be fash-

37.text: ioned into a sledge-runner. He wanted to strike the victor upon the head

38.text: with the wood; but the latter succeeded in catching hold of it by the

39.text: other end, and in wrenching it from the hands of his assailant. He threw it

40.text: away; then, incensed by the attack, he kicked his adversary in the face, just

41.text: as described in folk-lore. The other one fell down, his face bleeding. Now,

42.text: the young man belonged to a strong family, with a number of uncles and

43.text: cousins: so the next day some of his people came to the camp of the offender.
